topic.title: SC Ruling on Creamy Layer Determination for OBCs

subtopics.title: 2026 SC ruling on creamy layer
subtopics.summary: In March 2026 the Supreme Court ruled that parental income alone cannot be the sole criterion for determining creamy layer status of OBCs. The Court found that children of government employees are assessed by parental rank or post, while children of PSU and private-sector employees are assessed mainly on parental income, and called this unequal. The Court favoured a post-based criterion across all sectors, while critics point to the absence of a uniform private-sector hierarchy and to the role of income in access to opportunities.
facts: Supreme Court ruled parental income alone cannot be the sole criterion for creamy layer status of OBCs (March 2026).
Creamy layer principle excludes socially and economically advanced OBC members from reservation benefits.
Children of government employees are evaluated on parental rank or post.
Children of PSU and private-sector employees are assessed primarily on parental income.
The Court called this unequal method inconsistent and a violation of the principle of equality.
Court proposed a post-based criterion (Group A, B, C or D) as the primary factor for PSU and private-sector parents.
Rank or position in employment reflects social status and influence better than income alone.
Critics: private sector lacks a uniform rank hierarchy, making post-based classification difficult.
Critics: high-income private-sector families could retain reservation benefits.

subtopics.title: Early history of caste-based reservation
subtopics.summary: The idea of caste-based reservation was first proposed in 1882, and separate electorates appeared under the 1909 Act. The 1951 First Amendment added Article 15(4) to legalise caste-based reservation, after the Champakam Dorairajan case had held such reservations violated Article 15. The 1953 Kalelkar Commission and the 1963 MR Balaji ruling, which kept reservation at 50%, shaped the early framework.
facts: 1882: caste-based reservation first proposed by William Hunter and Jyotirao Phule.
1909: Government of India Act gave elements of reservation through separate electorates.
1932: MacDonald/Communal Award provided separate electorates for Depressed Classes.
Poona Pact abandoned separate electorates for Depressed Classes.
1935: Government of India Act extended separate electorates to Depressed Classes, Women and Labour.
1951: First Constitutional Amendment added Article 15(4).
Champakam Dorairajan vs State of Madras (1951): caste-based reservations held to violate Article 15.
1953: Kalelkar Commission (first Backward Class Commission) identified backward classes other than SCs and STs at national level.
1963: MR Balaji vs State of Mysore: Government ordered to keep reservation at 50%.

subtopics.title: Mandal Commission and Indra Sawhney case
subtopics.summary: In 1979 the Morarji Desai government appointed the second Backward Classes Commission under Article 340, and its 1980 report identified 3,743 castes and recommended 27% reservation in government jobs for OBCs. That recommendation was implemented in 1990, and in 1991 economic criteria were introduced along with a further 10% for poorer higher castes. The Indra Sawhney judgement of 1992 rejected the 10% but upheld the 27% OBC quota with conditions.
facts: 1979: Morarji Desai government appointed the second Backward Classes Commission under Article 340.
The commission was headed by BP Mandal and submitted its report in 1980.
Identified 3,743 castes as socially and educationally backward.
Recommended 27% reservation in government jobs for OBCs.
1990: 27% OBC reservation implemented by the VP Singh government.
1991: preference to poorer OBC sections and 10% reservation for economically backward higher castes.
Indra Sawhney (1992): the extra 10% for higher castes was rejected; 27% OBC reservation was upheld with conditions.
Conditions: total reservation shall not exceed 50%; reservation in promotions not allowed.
Creamy layer introduced and to be excluded while identifying Backward Classes; carry-forward rule for backlog vacancies valid.
A permanent statutory body should examine complaints of over- and under-inclusion in the OBC list.

subtopics.title: Later judgements and economic reservation
subtopics.summary: Later judgements clarified rules on promotions, the 9th Schedule and creamy layer exclusion for SCs and STs. The 103rd Constitutional Amendment of 2019 introduced 10% reservation for EWS, and the 2022 Janhit Abhiyan judgement upheld it. The 106th Amendment Act of 2023 provides one-third reservation for women in Parliament and State Legislatures, which ceases after 15 years.
facts: 2006 Nagaraj case: State not bound to provide reservation in promotions to SCs and STs.
To make such a provision, a State must collect quantifiable data, prove inadequate representation and show no compromise on efficiency.
2007 IR Coelho case: laws placed in the 9th Schedule after 24 April 1973 are subject to judicial review.
Tamil Nadu's 69% reservation policy was placed in the 9th Schedule in 1994 by the 76th Amendment Act.
2018 Jarnail Singh case: creamy layer exclusion extends to SCs and STs.
2018 Jarnail Singh case: reservation in promotions does not require quantifiable data on SC/ST backwardness.
103rd Constitutional Amendment (2019) provided 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS).
EWS reservation was based on a commission for Economically Backward Classes (constituted 2005, report July 2010).
2022 Janhit Abhiyan vs Union of India: 103rd Amendment upheld.
106th Amendment Act (2023): one-third of seats for women in Parliament and State Legislatures; ceases after 15 years.

subtopics.title: National Commission for Backward Classes
subtopics.summary: The National Commission for Backward Classes was set up in 1993 by an Act of Parliament. The 102nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 2018 gave it constitutional status under Article 338B and widened its functions. It consists of a Chairperson, a Vice-Chairperson and three other members, appointed by the President.
facts: Set up in 1993 by an Act of Parliament.
102nd Constitutional Amendment Act 2018 gave constitutional status to the NCBC.
Article 338B provided constitutional status to the NCBC and increased the scope of its functions.
NCBC is authorised to investigate complaints and welfare of backward classes.
Article 342A empowers the President to specify socially and educationally backward classes in States and UTs.
Composition: Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and 3 other members.
Members are appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal.
Conditions of service and tenure are determined by the President.
NCBC can recommend inclusion and exclusion of castes from the OBC list.
NCBC can recommend the income level that excludes the creamy layer from reservation benefits.

quizzes.title: Creamy layer ruling: MCQ set
quizzes.passage:
In March 2026, the Supreme Court of India ruled that parental income alone cannot be the sole criterion for determining the creamy layer status of Other Backward Classes (OBCs). The judgement responds to a concern about consistency in how the creamy layer is determined. The Court pointed to an uneven system in which children of government employees are assessed on the basis of parental rank or post, while children of employees in public sector undertakings and the private sector are assessed mainly on parental income. It described this unequal method as inconsistent and in conflict with the principle of equality.

The Court's reasoning rests on the view that rank or position in employment reflects social status and influence better than income alone. It also observed that long years of service may raise salary levels without necessarily improving social standing, especially for lower-level employees. A post-based criterion applied across all sectors could, in its view, provide a fair and consistent way to identify the creamy layer.

The ruling has drawn criticism. Private-sector employers have no standardised rank hierarchy, which makes post-based classification difficult. Critics also argue that income strongly shapes access to quality education and opportunities, and that high-income families in the private sector could keep reservation benefits, limiting opportunities for economically weaker OBC groups.

questions.q: A family is treated as creamy layer if its annual income exceeds what amount, and for how many consecutive years?
questions.explanation: A family is classified as creamy layer if its annual income exceeds 8 lakh for 3 consecutive years.

questions.q: Which 2018 judgement held that creamy layer exclusion extends to SCs and STs?
options: Jarnail Singh vs Lachhmi Narain Gupta case
questions.explanation: The Jarnail Singh vs Lachhmi Narain Gupta case (2018) held that creamy layer exclusion extends to SCs and STs.

questions.q: In the Champakam Dorairajan vs State of Madras (1951) case, what did the Court rule?
options: Caste-based reservations are valid under Article 15
Economic criteria must be used for reservation
Caste-based reservations are in violation of Article 15
questions.explanation: The Court ruled that caste-based reservations are in violation of Article 15.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Supreme Court in the Nagaraj case (2006) held that the State was not bound to provide reservation in promotions to SCs and STs.
Reason (R): Tamil Nadu's 69% reservation policy was placed under the 9th Schedule in 1994.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but the 1994 Tamil Nadu placement under the 9th Schedule does not explain the Nagaraj holding.

questions.q:
Match List I with List II:
I. Kalelkar Commission   ->   A. Identified 3,743 castes
II. Mandal (second Backward Classes) Commission   ->   B. Upheld the 103rd Constitutional Amendment (EWS)
III. Nagaraj case (2006)   ->   C. State not bound to provide reservation in promotions
IV. Janhit Abhiyan case (2022)   ->   D. Identified backward classes other than SCs and STs at national level
questions.explanation: The Kalelkar Commission identified backward classes other than SCs and STs, the Mandal Commission identified 3,743 castes, Nagaraj addressed promotions and Janhit Abhiyan upheld EWS reservation.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Indra Sawhney judgement (1992):
I. Reservation in promotions was permitted for OBCs.
II. The Creamy Layer was introduced and must be excluded while identifying Backward Classes.
III. Total reservation could exceed 50% in special cases.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: The judgement barred reservation in promotions and capped total reservation at 50%, leaving only the creamy layer statement correct.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Indra Sawhney judgement (1992):
I. It upheld 27% reservation for OBCs with conditions.
II. It upheld the additional 10% reservation for poorer sections of higher castes.
III. It introduced the concept of Creamy Layer.
IV. It upheld the carry forward rule for unfilled vacancies.
How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation: The judgement rejected the extra 10% for higher castes, so statements I, III and IV are the three correct ones.

questions.q: In which Schedule of the Constitution was Tamil Nadu's 69% reservation policy placed in 1994?
questions.explanation: The 1994 76th Amendment Act placed Tamil Nadu's 69% reservation policy under the 9th Schedule.

quizzes.title: Mandal Commission and Indra Sawhney: numbers
quizzes.passage:
After independence, the government recognised that some communities beyond the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes remained socially and educationally backward. A later Backward Classes Commission was set up under a constitutional provision that allows the state to investigate the conditions of such classes and suggest measures for their advancement. Its work involved studying the social standing of these communities across the country before recommending remedies.

The Commission's central recommendation concerned reservation in government jobs for backward communities. The government of the time later implemented this recommendation, and the decision set off a national debate on social justice and the share of seats reserved for these groups.

In a later judgement, the Supreme Court examined the validity of the reservation. It upheld the scheme with conditions. These included a limit on the total reserved share, a bar on reservation in promotions, and a requirement that advanced members of the class be excluded. The Court also held that the carry-forward rule for backlog vacancies could remain valid, and it called for a permanent statutory body to handle complaints about inclusion in the list.

questions.q: Under which Article of the Constitution was the second Backward Classes Commission set up? (give the number only)
questions.explanation: The commission was appointed in 1979 in terms of Article 340 of the Constitution.

questions.q: In which year did this commission submit its report?
questions.explanation: The commission submitted its report in 1980 after its 1979 appointment.

questions.q: How many castes did the commission identify as socially and educationally backward?
questions.explanation: The commission identified 3,743 castes as socially and educationally backward.

questions.q: What percentage of government jobs did the commission recommend for OBCs? (in per cent)
questions.explanation: The commission recommended 27% reservation in government jobs for Other Backward Classes.

questions.q: Which Prime Minister's government appointed the commission in 1979?
questions.explanation: The Morarji Desai government appointed the second Backward Classes Commission in 1979.

questions.q: In 1991, what percentage of jobs was reserved for economically backward sections of higher castes not covered by any existing scheme? (in per cent)
questions.explanation: The 1991 government reserved another 10% of jobs for poorer sections of higher castes not covered by any existing scheme.

questions.q: Under the Indra Sawhney judgement, what was the ceiling on total reservation? (in per cent)
questions.explanation: The judgement stated that reservation shall not exceed 50%.
